title: Adelaide University Exchange Study Experience
paragraphs: Nurse: "Hey, are you the one in charge of the patient in that bed over there?" Me: "Y-yes... what is it?" Nurse: "Could you prescribe a drug? I think they need a painkiller." Me: "What, but... I don't know. I'll ask the doctor (sweat)."

This conversation happened almost every day during my clerkship in an Australian hospital. The nurses ask me everything, from drug prescriptions and IV fluids to treatment plans and expected discharge, as soon as they know I am in charge. This is because in Australia sixth-year medical students are considered to have almost the same ability as doctors. Australian medical schools have no general education; students begin studying medicine from the first year, hospital clerkships start in the third year, and they take the national examination at the end of the fifth year. So by the time local medical students reach the sixth year, their knowledge and skills are almost on a par with doctors. In particular, the partner university that looked after me this time, the University of Adelaide (located in Adelaide, the capital of South Australia, with an atmosphere like Nagoya), apparently has the philosophy that "medicine cannot improve without conversation with patients," and many departments leave history taking and examination of patients entirely to medical students, so every department was very instructive. Among them, I would like to write about the "rural medicine" clerkship, which left the greatest impression on me. At the University of Adelaide, fifth-year students can choose whether to do their one year of clinical clerkships at a large hospital in the city or at a small clinic in a remote area. The students who choose remote areas are divided into groups of about four and assigned to about 15 remote locations. There they do their clerkships for one year while living together in shared housing. A real Terrace House. This time I was allowed to do a one-month clerkship in Cadina, a small town of 6,000 people three hours by car from Adelaide, one of the 15 remote locations where the fifth-year students were staying.

In Cadina there is one small clinic and one small hospital (about 30 beds). On the first day of the clerkship at Cadina Clinic, I found myself seated in an outpatient room, and in front of me was a patient complaining of back pain. As you will have noticed, in the rural medicine clerkship medical students have to run the outpatient clinic as well. Of course, I had no outpatient experience at all, so while looking things up in textbooks and on the internet and consulting the doctor between consultations, I flustered through history taking and examination, ordering tests and prescribing drugs, and before I knew it it was 6:30 p.m., closing time. But this was not the end. After the outpatient clinic at the clinic, examining emergency patients in the hospital's ER awaited. I went to the hospital at 8 p.m., when the late-night hours began, and examined patients until there were none left. Even though I thought I was doing my best through the exhaustion, my knowledge and skills were inferior to those of the Australian students, so I was often scolded. The first week was truly hard both physically and mentally, and I cried every day, wondering what on earth I was doing in this damn countryside full of eucalyptus, where there are more sheep than people, wanting to go back to Japan quickly, or rather, to go back to the city of Adelaide. But in that first week, I realized that I was getting experience equal to, or even greater than, the two months of clerkships in the city of Adelaide up to then. In the outpatient clinic I learned a wide range of care, from controlling diabetes and hypertension to a child's ligament injury and breaking the news of cancer, and in the ER I learned not only the treatment of extremely urgent diseases such as aortic dissection and acute myocardial infarction but also how to suture casually without sterile gloves and how to remove a fishhook stuck in a finger, and in my private time I did a mysterious pair dance with the fifth-year students at a festival celebrating immigrants from Britain... Since I was being given this much experience, I thought I must not complain, and that rather I had to grow quickly so as to be able to help the doctors, and I was able to keep running for the remaining three weeks.

All of this is thanks to the doctors, who entrusted me with a lot of work and taught me everything by hand, the patients, who trusted a good-for-nothing medical student who could hardly speak English, the nurses, who corrected my shaky practice from the side, the students, who, concerned about my state, invited me to play and study, my host family, who made delicious meals that blew away the fatigue of the clerkship, and the residents of Cadina, who smilingly picked up a suspicious Asian hitchhiking (20 km to the hospital, no trains). My gratitude to everyone in Cadina is so great that I did not know how to express it and I even burst into tears on the last day.

For me it was such a big experience that I cannot talk about my study abroad without rural medicine. I really feel glad I chose it. If you ask whether I want to go back again, the answer is No (laughs). The Australian outback is a place that tests physical strength, mental strength and communication skills. Juniors, please do take up the challenge!
